entries.name: 155mm Artillery Shell Reconstitution
entries.thesisShort: The US is still trying to triple 155mm shell output and is not close: production was about 36,000 rounds per month as of March 2026 against a 100,000 goal, with General Dynamics owning the largest slice of the projectile and propellant chain.
entries.thesisLong:
The 155mm artillery shell is the clearest physical bottleneck in Western defense, and 2026 has made the scale of the shortfall harder to argue with rather than easier.

The Army's goal was 100,000 rounds per month by October 2025. As of March 2026 it was producing about 36,000 rounds per month — below the roughly 40,000 per month rate the industrial base had already reached, not above it. A July 2026 Army Inspector General report examined why billions of dollars of investment have not converted into rounds.

The specific failure is instructive because it sits inside General Dynamics. The Mesquite, Texas facility operated by GD Ordnance and Tactical Systems, opened in May 2024, failed to produce any of the 30,000 projectile metal parts per month it was expected to make, and an Army official was publicly described as 'not happy' with GD's handling of the contract in February 2026. Metal parts are upstream of everything: load-assemble-pack capacity is useless without bodies to fill.

The capacity that does exist is real. GD's new load, assemble and pack facility in Camden, Arkansas is designed to produce 50,000 completed high-explosive projectiles per month at full rate. The question the next several quarters answer is whether the projectile metal parts supply catches up to the LAP capacity, or whether Camden runs starved.

That gap is the investment-relevant fact here, and it cuts both ways: it is the reason demand and appropriations keep flowing, and the reason revenue recognition keeps slipping. General Dynamics as a whole is not short of work — Q2 2026 total backlog reached a record $136.5 billion, up 32% year over year — but this specific programme is behind.

entries.name: Javelin & Next-Gen Anti-Armor Missiles
entries.thesisShort: The Lockheed-RTX Javelin joint venture completed its supply-chain re-engineering in March 2026 and is now ramping from about 2,400 missiles a year toward 3,960 by late 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
The Javelin Joint Venture between Lockheed Martin and RTX produces roughly 2,400 missiles per year and is in the middle of a capacity expansion to 3,960 per year by late 2026 — a 65% increase intended to serve Ukraine restocks, US Army inventory and NATO demand simultaneously.

The important 2026 development is that the hard part is finished. On 26 March 2026 Lockheed announced that the Javelin supply chain had completed its non-recurring engineering work — additional tooling, test sets and in some cases expanded floor space. Nearly 100 part-level suppliers and 25 major subcontractors spent eight to ten months completing the required updates, and the full production ramp is expected to begin later in the year. That is the sequencing that separates a real munitions ramp from an announced one: the supply base has to be re-qualified before the prime can build faster, and it now has been.

Manufacturing upgrades span Troy and Huntsville in Alabama and Ocala in Florida. Propulsion capacity is being expanded in parallel: L3Harris won a record $292 million five-year contract in September 2025 to expand Javelin motor output, investing in new Virginia factories and automation. RTX delivered the first Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units to the US Army in May 2026.

The risks have shifted from industrial to strategic. Loitering munitions are partially displacing anti-armor missiles in the roles Javelin was designed for, and a Ukraine ceasefire would reduce the urgency behind restock orders just as the expanded capacity comes online — the classic timing risk in any munitions ramp.

entries.name: Patriot/PAC-3 Air & Missile Defense
entries.thesisShort: PAC-3 MSE is under a seven-year framework agreement signed in January 2026 to lift production from 600 missiles a year to 2,000 by 2030, backed by a $4.7 billion acceleration contract in April 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Patriot is the most-demanded air defense system on the planet, and the interceptor — not the radar or the launcher — is the binding constraint. Lockheed Martin builds the PAC-3 MSE; RTX builds the radar, launcher and ground system, which is why this bottleneck spans two primes.

The commitment moved from intention to contract in 2026. Lockheed delivered 620 PAC-3 MSEs in 2025, more than 20% above the prior year, and production has risen more than 60% over the past two years. In January 2026 the Pentagon and Lockheed signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise output from 600 missiles annually to 2,000 a year by 2030, and on 10 April 2026 Lockheed announced a $4.7 billion contract to accelerate production. An earlier October 2024 award funds the intermediate step to 650 per year, expected by 2027.

The honest read on the ramp is that it is heavily back-loaded. Going from roughly 620 to 650 by 2027 is a 5% increase; going from 650 to 2,000 by 2030 is a tripling compressed into three years, and Lockheed's CEO has framed it as a phased ramp across factories and the supply chain. Everything that has historically constrained interceptor output — seekers, solid rocket motors, energetics, skilled labour — has to scale at once.

Demand is not the question. European Sky Shield participants, Gulf states rebuilding inventory after live engagements, and US war reserve requirements all compete for the same production line, which creates an allocation tension between American stocks and foreign military sales that intensifies as the ramp proceeds.

entries.name: Submarine Shipyard Capacity (Newport News)
entries.thesisShort: HII's Newport News is one of only two US yards qualified to build nuclear submarines, and Q2 2026 brought roughly $76.6 billion of additional Virginia- and Columbia-class contract modifications, lifting total backlog to $57.3 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
HII's Newport News Shipbuilding is one of only two US yards qualified to build nuclear submarines, and the entire Virginia-class and Columbia-class pipeline runs through it alongside General Dynamics Electric Boat. There is no third option and no path to creating one inside a decade.

Q2 2026 was a step change in contracted work. Roughly $76.6 billion of additional Virginia-class and Columbia-class contract modifications were announced for Newport News, including about $25 billion of Virginia-class work and $5.5 billion for Columbia. New contract awards in the quarter were $6.7 billion, taking total backlog to $57.3 billion as of 30 June 2026. Revenue was $3,418 million with net income of $208 million, or $5.27 per diluted share, and management raised full-year 2026 shipbuilding revenue guidance to $10.2-10.4 billion with shipbuilding operating margin guidance of 6-6.5%.

Delivery is the part that lags contracting, and always has. The Virginia-class SSN-800 Arkansas is progressing toward delivery later this year, and HII plans to deliver five ships over the next twelve months including three from Ingalls. The Navy wants a sustained two Virginia-class boats per year; the industrial base has not yet reached it.

The binding constraint is people. Nuclear shipbuilding requires welders, pipefitters and electricians trained to standards that take years to reach, and the workforce gap — not funding and no longer contract coverage — is what determines whether the delivery rate rises. Cost growth on first-in-class Columbia work remains the other live exposure.

entries.name: Electric Boat & Combat Systems
entries.thesisShort: GD's Electric Boat is prime on both Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines, and Q2 2026 showed the ramp working: Columbia hours earned rose 37% year over year with sequence-critical material deliveries up 65%.
entries.thesisLong:
General Dynamics Electric Boat is the prime contractor for both the Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarine programmes and shares the nuclear-qualified industrial base with HII's Newport News. Marine Systems has become the segment that carries the company.

Q2 2026 Marine Systems revenue was $4.7 billion, up 10.4% year over year, led by volume on Columbia and Virginia-class, with segment operating earnings up 17.5% and operating margin up 40 basis points. Total General Dynamics backlog reached a record $136.5 billion, up 32% year over year.

The operational detail matters more than the revenue line, because submarine programmes have historically announced progress they could not sustain. At Electric Boat, hours earned on Columbia rose 37% versus the same period last year across the first half of 2026, and sequence-critical material deliveries rose 65% against Q2 2025. Hours earned measures work actually completed rather than work scheduled, and sequence-critical material is the specific category whose absence stops a hull — so both metrics point at the same conclusion: the constraint is loosening rather than the schedule being restated.

Management says it remains on track for the goal of two Virginia-class submarines and one Columbia-class per year by the early 2030s. That is the number the Navy needs and the number the industrial base has repeatedly missed, which is why the intermediate operating indicators carry the weight here.

Risks remain first-of-class cost growth on Columbia, single-point-of-failure suppliers, AUKUS commitments competing with domestic schedules, and the same skilled-trades shortage HII faces.

entries.name: GE Aerospace Military Engines (F404/F414/T901)
entries.thesisShort: GE Aerospace's Defense & Propulsion Technologies segment grew Q2 2026 orders 12% and revenue 16% year over year, with backlog above $30 billion after new engine programme wins.
entries.thesisLong:
GE Aerospace's Defense & Propulsion Technologies segment supplies the F414 (Super Hornet, KAAN, Tejas, Gripen) and the T901 (Apache and Black Hawk), engines that sit at the centre of Western and allied re-armament.

Q2 2026 showed the segment carrying more of the company. DPT orders rose 12% year over year, revenue rose 16%, and operating profit grew 18% to $475 million. Segment backlog stands above $30 billion following new engine programme wins — the visibility that lets a propulsion business invest ahead of demand rather than chase it.

The India F414 story is the largest single swing factor and has been in negotiation for nearly three years. GE Aerospace and Hindustan Aeronautics have reported progress toward finalising F414 assembly in India, with engines to be co-produced there to power the HAL Tejas Mk2. Technology transfer terms are what the talks turn on, and they have slipped repeatedly — anyone underwriting this entry should treat closure as unresolved rather than imminent.

The T901 is the other programme to watch. GE has expedited T901 development for the US Army and reduced its cost despite programme uncertainty, and the improved turbine engine is the retrofit path for a very large existing rotorcraft fleet.

The structural risk is unchanged: Pratt & Whitney holds the F-35 propulsion monopoly, which locks GE out of the single largest Western fighter programme, and adaptive engine funding remains uncertain. Supply chain constraints on backlog burn are the operational counterweight to a $30 billion order book.

entries.name: Pratt & Whitney F135 (F-35 Engine)
entries.thesisShort: Pratt & Whitney holds the F-35 propulsion monopoly and definitized $6.6 billion of Lots 18-19 production in March 2026 — but a government watchdog now says the Engine Core Upgrade will not begin production until at least 2031.
entries.thesisLong:
Pratt & Whitney has the F-35 propulsion monopoly, and there is no second source: the alternate engine programme was cancelled long ago and the adaptive engine competitors were never funded to production. Every F-35 built for the rest of the programme's life carries an F135.

The production book has been filling. Pratt & Whitney was awarded a $6.6 billion contract in March 2026 to definitize Lots 18-19, including a $3.8 billion modification, and in July 2026 received a further $1.3 billion undefinitized contract for F135 spare parts — funding fiscal 2026 initial spares, deployable spare packages, depot lay-ins and support equipment for US and international F-35 customers. Sustainment, not production, is where the long-duration economics of this franchise sit.

The Engine Core Upgrade is the piece that has moved materially, and in the wrong direction. ECU is the selected propulsion modernisation solution for the F-35 and the enabler for Block 4 capability, and it leverages the existing F135 sustainment network. But a government watchdog report now says the programme will not begin production until at least 2031. Anyone treating ECU as a near-term production catalyst is working from an outdated schedule; it is a decade-scale programme whose revenue arrives in the 2030s.

That pushes the near-term question back onto delivery performance. Engine deliveries have historically gated the F-35 airframe rate, and Lockheed's own guidance assumes a sustained 156 aircraft per year — a rate that requires Pratt to keep pace. Supplier fragility on single-source castings and forgings, plus sustainment cost growth pressuring the Pentagon, are the other live exposures.

entries.name: F-35 Airframe & Block 4 Modernization
entries.thesisShort: Lockheed has now delivered 1,344 production F-35s and holds a 317-aircraft backlog, but 1H 2026 deliveries of 51 jets run well below the 156-per-year rate its guidance assumes.
entries.thesisLong:
The F-35 is the largest Western fighter programme and Lockheed Martin is its sole airframer. Through 28 June 2026 the company had delivered 1,344 production aircraft since programme inception — 956 F-35As, 250 F-35Bs and 138 F-35Cs — with a backlog of 317 aircraft.

The delivery cadence is the number that changed. Lockheed delivered 32 F-35s in Q1 2026 and 19 in Q2 2026, for 51 across the first half. Guidance assumes a sustained production rate of 156 aircraft per year, so the first half tracks meaningfully below the annualised rate — a normal consequence of the record 2025 year having cleared a TR-3-induced backlog that will not repeat, but a gap that has to close in the second half.

The company itself is performing. Q2 2026 sales rose 11% year over year to $20.1 billion, backlog reached a record $230 billion, and EPS was $7.94, with the uplift driven primarily by higher F-35 production volume in Aeronautics.

The backlog figure also moved: 317 aircraft against the 416 carried previously, which is what happens when deliveries outpace new orders for a period. It remains multiple years of production, but the direction is worth tracking rather than assuming.

Risks are the familiar programme set: cost per flight hour above target, engine deliveries from Pratt & Whitney gating the airframe rate, sustainment cost under political scrutiny, and the loss of the NGAD prime position, which removes Lockheed from the next-generation air dominance airframe.

entries.name: HEICO Aftermarket & Mission-Critical Components
entries.thesisShort: HEICO is the dominant FAA-approved aftermarket parts manufacturer with a compounding defense electronics arm; fiscal Q2 2026 delivered record net income up 49% on 18% consolidated organic sales growth.
entries.thesisLong:
HEICO occupies an unusual seat in aerospace: it manufactures FAA-approved replacement parts under Parts Manufacturer Approval, selling into an aftermarket the original equipment makers would prefer to keep, and it pairs that with a defense electronics business that compounds quietly through missile defense and ISR demand.

Fiscal Q2 2026 was a record across the board — net income of $233.8 million, up 49% from $156.8 million a year earlier, on record operating income up 41% and record net sales up 25%. What makes the quarter notable is the composition: 18% consolidated organic net sales growth, meaning the majority of the increase came from the existing business rather than from the acquisitions HEICO closes at a steady cadence.

The Electronic Technologies Group grew 17% organically, driven by demand for defense, aerospace and space products alongside other electronics. That is the segment that connects this entry to the defense bottleneck rather than to the commercial aftermarket cycle — missile defense and space programmes need qualified electronics, and qualification is a multi-year barrier that protects incumbents.

The Flight Support side benefits from a structurally aging global airline fleet, since older aircraft consume more replacement parts and operators become more price-sensitive about them — precisely the conditions under which PMA penetration rises.

Risks include commercial aerospace traffic cyclicality, OEM pushback on PMA penetration, and integration execution across a continuous tuck-in acquisition programme.

entries.name: Rocket Lab Launch & Spacecraft Manufacturing
entries.thesisShort: Rocket Lab posted record Q2 2026 revenue of $234 million and a record $2.36 billion backlog, but Neutron has still never flown — the target is delivery to the pad in Q4 2026 with no confirmed first-flight date.
entries.thesisLong:
Rocket Lab is the only Western pure-play small and medium launcher with demonstrated cadence, and 2026 has separated the company's commercial momentum from its central technical milestone.

The commercial side is compounding fast. Q2 2026 revenue was a record $234 million, up 62% year over year, and backlog reached a record $2.36 billion — now exceeding 90 launches — with more than $437 million of new launch contracts in the quarter and over $1 billion of new contracts already signed in Q3 across launch and space systems, including a $397 million Space Force award. Rocket Lab has also been consolidating the stack around itself, closing the Mynaric and Motiv acquisitions and announcing an agreement to acquire Iridium Communications, which would move it from launch and components into operating an on-orbit constellation and its revenue.

Neutron is the milestone that has not happened. As of August 2026 the vehicle has never flown. Production of the Stage 1 tank is aligned with a target of delivering Neutron to the launch pad in Q4 2026, but the company has not confirmed a first-flight date — and delivery to the pad is not a launch. The $50 million-plus medium-lift market that Neutron is meant to open remains dominated by SpaceX until it flies.

So the entry now reads as two businesses: a space systems and small-launch operation with real backlog and accelerating revenue, and an option on medium lift that has been repeatedly deferred. The risks are further Neutron slippage into 2027, competition from Vulcan and New Glenn, and integration of an acquisition programme that has grown considerably in ambition.

entries.name: AST SpaceMobile BlueBird Direct-to-Cell
entries.thesisShort: AST SpaceMobile reached 13 satellites in orbit after launching six in under 50 days, and reiterated 2026 revenue guidance of $150-200 million while targeting 45 satellites by early 2027.
entries.thesisLong:
AST SpaceMobile is building the only space-based cellular broadband network designed to work with unmodified phones, a capability the Pentagon has funded explicitly as a backup to terrestrial communications.

Deployment has accelerated sharply. The in-orbit total reached 13 satellites after six spacecraft were launched in under 50 days. BlueBirds 14, 15 and 16 are close to shipment-ready, satellites 17 through 46 are at various points in the production and assembly pipeline, and the company is scaling manufacturing toward a target of six satellites per month — the rate that supports having 45 satellites in orbit by early 2027. Launch cadence, not manufacturing, has historically been this company's constraint, and six launches in under 50 days is the first evidence that it has eased.

The financial picture is earlier-stage than the deployment picture. Q2 2026 revenue was $31.5 million, more than double Q1, but below the roughly $34.5 million analysts expected. Full-year guidance of $150-200 million was reiterated, which requires a substantial second-half acceleration. Contracted revenue backlog stands at approximately $1.30 billion across commercial partners and US Government awards.

Funding took a meaningful non-dilutive step: AST received a preliminary award under Japan's JLEO low-earth-orbit satellite infrastructure programme with long-time partner Rakuten, carrying up to roughly $1 billion in non-dilutive, non-debt government capital. For a capital-intensive constellation build, the source of funding matters as much as the amount.

The company is targeting a beta service launch with certain mobile network partners before year-end 2026. Risks remain Starlink direct-to-device competition, the capital intensity of reaching global coverage, and the gap between $31.5 million of quarterly revenue and a $150-200 million annual guide.

entries.name: MP Materials Mine-to-Magnet Vertical Integration
entries.thesisShort: MP Materials runs the only fully integrated rare earth mine-to-magnet operation in North America; Q2 2026 NdPr production rose 41% to 840 metric tons with first commercial magnet deliveries expected in Q4 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
MP Materials operates Mountain Pass, the only rare earth mine in the United States, and is building the only fully integrated mine-to-magnet chain in North America. The Department of Defense named it the primary domestic supplier for NdFeB magnets, and the economics of that relationship are unusual: a ten-year $110 per kilogram NdPr price floor that protects qualifying production against Chinese price suppression. That floor is the single most important structural feature of this entry, because Chinese producers have repeatedly used price to prevent Western capacity from reaching scale.

Q2 2026 showed the upstream working. Revenue rose 89% year over year to $108.5 million on higher NdPr sales and improved pricing, and adjusted EBITDA swung to a positive $28.5 million, a $41.0 million year-over-year improvement, helped by price protection agreement income. NdPr production reached 840 metric tons, up 41%, with sales volumes up 127% to 1,006 metric tons and Q3 production expected to exceed 1,000 metric tons.

Downstream is where the transition cost shows. Magnetics segment revenue was $16.5 million, down 17% year over year, reflecting the Independence facility's shift toward commercial magnet production. Customer qualification with GM advanced during the quarter and initial commercial magnet deliveries are expected in Q4 2026, with production ramping thereafter. Construction continues on the 10X facility.

MP also entered a long-term offtake for separated gadolinium with a leading US aerospace and defense customer, extending the product portfolio into heavy rare earths — historically the gap in the US position, since Mountain Pass is a light rare earth deposit.

Risks are execution-shaped: magnet qualification and ramp, customer concentration, 10X construction timeline, and Chinese pricing behaviour testing the floor mechanism.

entries.name: USA Rare Earth Heavy REE & Stillwater Magnets
entries.thesisShort: USA Rare Earth is targeting a 600 metric ton per annum magnet run-rate at Stillwater in Q4 2026, doubling to 1,200 in Q1 2027, while the Round Top heavy rare earth feasibility study runs to a Q4 2026 completion.
entries.thesisLong:
USA Rare Earth is the second pillar of the US rare earth position and addresses the gap MP Materials does not: heavy rare earths, specifically dysprosium and terbium, which are required for magnets that hold their strength at high temperature — the ones in defense actuators and traction motors.

The Stillwater magnet facility is the near-term asset. The company expects to reach a 600 metric ton per annum run-rate of magnet manufacturing capacity there in Q4 2026 under Phase 1a, with a Phase 1b expansion to 1,200 metric tons total in Q1 2027. That is a materially more modest and more specific figure than the eventual 4,800 metric ton design capacity, and the phased framing is the more useful one for tracking execution.

Round Top, the heavy rare earth deposit in Texas, is still pre-development. The Definitive Feasibility Study is expected to complete in Q4 2026 with publication in Q1 2027 — meaning the resource that defines the long-term thesis will not have a completed feasibility study until the end of this year. Additional funding includes a $14.2 million grant from the Texas Semiconductor Innovation Fund for Round Top development.

Capital deployment is heavy relative to revenue. Q2 2026 capital expenditures were approximately $66 million, supporting expansion across multiple facilities, and the quarter carried a revenue miss. This remains a construction-and-permitting story funded substantially by federal and state policy support, not an operating business.

Risks are concentrated accordingly: the aggressive pull-forward of production timelines, capital needs against the cash position, Round Top permitting after the DFS, and dependence on continued policy support.

entries.name: Palantir Maven & TITAN — Defense AI Operating System
entries.thesisShort: Palantir is the de facto AI operating system for the US military; Q2 2026 revenue grew 93% year over year to $1.94 billion with US government revenue up 90% to $809 million.
entries.thesisLong:
Palantir has become the software layer through which the US military plans, targets and manages logistics, and 2026 has been the year the growth rate stopped looking like enterprise software and started looking like infrastructure adoption.

Q2 2026 revenue was $1.94 billion, up 93% year over year. US government revenue grew 90% to $809 million — notable because government was already the mature half of the business, and re-accelerating a mature segment to 90% growth is harder than growing a new one. US commercial revenue grew 149%, with remaining deal value of $6.24 billion, more than double a year ago.

Deal activity broadened rather than concentrating: 220 deals worth $1 million or more closed in the quarter, including 98 above $5 million and 70 above $10 million. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $8.15-8.16 billion from a prior $7.65-7.66 billion, a mid-year increase of roughly half a billion dollars.

The bottleneck framing holds because of what the software does rather than what it sells for. Programme-of-record status means the Pentagon's targeting and logistics workflows are built on top of Palantir rather than integrated with it, and replacing that is a multi-year undertaking no competitor has demonstrated. The consolidation of many separate contracts into enterprise-wide agreements deepens that position further.

The exposures are structural rather than operational: dependence on defense budget priorities and the current administration's AI posture, key-person concentration, and pricing pressure as the Pentagon seeks more capability per dollar from a supplier it now depends on.
catalysts: Full-year 2026 guidance raised by roughly $500M mid-year
US government revenue re-accelerating to 90% growth
Enterprise agreements consolidating fragmented programme contracts
NATO and allied software adoption
risks: Dependence on defense budget priorities and current AI policy posture
Key-person concentration
Pricing pressure as the Pentagon seeks more capability per dollar
Growth rate creating a high bar for subsequent comparisons

entries.name: CrowdStrike Federal Zero Trust & DoW Cyber
entries.thesisShort: CrowdStrike carries FedRAMP High and DoD IL-5 authorization and has extended FedRAMP High to Falcon for XIoT, reaching total ARR of $5.51 billion, up 24% year over year.
entries.thesisLong:
CrowdStrike's Falcon platform holds FedRAMP High authorization and DoD Impact Level 5 accreditation, the two clearances that determine whether a commercial security product can be deployed on sensitive federal and defense networks at all. Those authorizations take years and are the actual moat — the technology competition is downstream of the paperwork.

The platform has extended further into federal infrastructure. CrowdStrike achieved FedRAMP High Authorization for Falcon for XIoT, taking the platform beyond endpoints into mission-critical federal operational technology and connected infrastructure. That matters because OT — industrial control systems, building systems, connected sensors at bases and facilities — is the part of the federal attack surface that zero-trust mandates reach last and that has almost no authorized commercial coverage.

At the company level, total annual recurring revenue reached $5.51 billion as of 30 April 2026, up 24% year over year. Federal is a subset of that rather than a separately disclosed line, so the federal thesis has to be read through authorizations and platform reach rather than through a reported revenue number — a genuine limitation on how precisely this entry can be tracked.

The competitive pressure is structural and comes from bundling: Microsoft Defender arrives inside E5 licences agencies already buy, which makes the procurement question a marginal-cost comparison rather than a capability comparison. Long federal procurement cycles and the litigation tail from the July 2024 outage remain the other exposures.

entries.name: Leidos ISR, Space Sensing & Air Defense
entries.thesisShort: Leidos carries a $48.7 billion backlog and won a Golden Dome award for sensor payloads on 18 additional missile warning and tracking satellites, with a Defense segment book-to-bill of 2.2 in Q2 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Leidos sits where ISR, space sensing and missile defense meet, and its Q2 2026 results show the Defense segment pulling far ahead of the services business it grew out of.

Revenue was $4.56 billion, up 7% year over year including 4% organically. Net bookings were $4.9 billion for a company-wide book-to-bill of 1.1, and backlog ended the quarter at $48.7 billion of which $10.2 billion was funded. The funded backlog figure is the one that moved: up 44% year over year against 5% growth in total backlog, meaning a much larger share of the book now carries appropriated money behind it rather than sitting as contract ceiling.

The Defense segment posted a 2.2 book-to-bill in the quarter and 1.9 on a trailing twelve-month basis — booking roughly twice what it billed. Leidos won the award to provide sensor payloads for an additional 18 missile warning and missile tracking satellites in support of Golden Dome, which is the programme now organising most US missile defense spending and the reason space sensing has become the segment's centre of gravity.

Management raised 2026 guidance: revenue midpoint by $100 million, EPS by $0.05 and operating cash flow by $50 million.

The structural tension in this business is unchanged. Services revenue carries mid-single-digit margins and competes against Booz Allen, SAIC and CACI on rate, while the differentiated hardware and sensing work carries the growth. Federal efficiency initiatives compress the former; execution risk on complex sensing and hypersonic programmes is the exposure on the latter.

entries.name: Kratos Valkyrie CCA & Tactical Drones
entries.thesisShort: Kratos' XQ-58 Valkyrie is the Marines' first Collaborative Combat Aircraft selection, with 15-20 aircraft due for delivery in 2026 and a plan to reach roughly 40 per year by the start of 2028.
entries.thesisLong:
Kratos built the XQ-58 Valkyrie on its own money before the Pentagon had settled what a Collaborative Combat Aircraft should be, and that bet has now been validated by the Marine Corps selecting it as their first CCA.

The production picture is concrete but still modest. Kratos expects to deliver 15-20 Valkyrie aircraft in 2026 as the Marine Corps prepares a contract award, and plans to begin producing approximately 40 Valkyries annually by the start of 2028. XQ-58s with built-in landing gear — the configuration that removes the rocket-assisted launch and parachute recovery constraint — are now in production, which is what makes higher sortie rates and conventional basing possible.

The company around the programme is growing faster than the programme itself. Q2 2026 revenue was $458.8 million, up 30.5% year over year, with GAAP net income of $4.4 million and an operating loss of $1.6 million. Unmanned Systems revenue was $79.1 million on 8.1% organic growth with Valkyrie the primary driver, though Unmanned Systems backlog was essentially flat at $374.6 million against $375.4 million the prior quarter. Consolidated bookings were $492.2 million for a 1.1 book-to-bill, total backlog $2.084 billion, and the bid pipeline $15.0 billion.

The flat Unmanned backlog alongside strong consolidated growth is the tension in this entry: Kratos is growing on its broader portfolio — targets, propulsion, space and C5ISR — while the Valkyrie programme still awaits contract definitization. Unit economics at 40 aircraft per year remain unproven, engine supply is a known constraint, and the company posted an operating loss on a 30% growth quarter.

entries.name: AeroVironment Switchblade & Loitering Munitions
entries.thesisShort: AeroVironment closed fiscal 2026 with $2.0 billion of revenue and funded backlog up to $1.2 billion after the BlueHalo acquisition, and guides fiscal 2027 to $2.125-2.225 billion.
entries.thesisLong:
AeroVironment is the dominant Western maker of small loitering munitions, and the BlueHalo acquisition has changed what the company is: no longer a Switchblade manufacturer with adjacent products, but a combined platform spanning loitering munitions, counter-UAS, directed energy and space.

Fiscal 2026, ended 30 April 2026, closed at $2.0 billion of revenue, with a fourth quarter of $641.6 million, up 133% year over year — of which acquisitions, principally BlueHalo and Empirical Systems Aerospace, contributed $282.3 million. Funded backlog climbed to $1.2 billion from $726.6 million a year earlier. Fiscal 2027 guidance is $2.125-2.225 billion of revenue with adjusted EBITDA of $305-325 million.

That guidance is the number to sit with. Growing from $2.0 billion to roughly $2.17 billion at the midpoint is high single digits — a marked deceleration from the acquisition-inflated fiscal 2026, and the point at which the combined company has to demonstrate organic growth rather than consolidation arithmetic.

Capacity is being built against a much larger opportunity than current volumes. The Salt Lake City manufacturing facility has the potential to produce more than $2 billion worth of Switchblades or other AV products per year — roughly the entire current revenue of the company from a single site — and the national manufacturing footprint now spans multiple states.

The competitive pressure is real and asymmetric. Chinese FPV drones deliver a fraction of the capability at a small fraction of the cost, and Anduril competes on autonomy software. Integration execution across the enlarged platform is the other live exposure.

entries.name: ATI Titanium & Specialty Aerospace Alloys
entries.thesisShort: ATI is the largest US producer of aerospace-grade titanium and specialty alloys; Q2 2026 brought a record $4.4 billion backlog and premium titanium lead times stretched to 20 months.
entries.thesisLong:
ATI melts and forms the titanium and nickel-based alloys that airframes, jet engines and missile structures are made from, and 2026 has been the year the constraint moved visibly upstream to the melt shop.

Q2 2026 revenue rose 11% year over year to $1,261.1 million, with aerospace and defense up 13%. Adjusted EBITDA grew 37% to $284.4 million and margin expanded 440 basis points to 22.6% on stronger commercial terms, favourable mix and operational improvement. Adjusted EPS was $1.23 against $0.74 a year earlier, and full-year guidance was raised across every key metric, to an adjusted EBITDA midpoint of $1,160 million and adjusted EPS midpoint of $5.04.

The bottleneck evidence is in two numbers. Backlog reached a record $4.4 billion, up 18% year over year, with roughly 70% expected to be fulfilled within twelve months — so this is near-dated committed work, not a distant option. And lead times for premium quality titanium have extended to 20 months. When a material takes nearly two years to obtain, it gates the airframe and engine rates downstream of it regardless of what those programmes are funded to build.

ATI is adding capacity into that gap, and the timing is imperfect: qualification at the new facility in Mexico and at the new titanium electron-beam furnace (EB2) shifted roughly $30-40 million of revenue into future periods. Qualification delay is the characteristic risk in specialty metals — the metal exists, the customer approval does not yet.

Risks include titanium price volatility, commercial aerospace cyclicality, and the energy intensity of vacuum melt operations.

entries.name: Carpenter Technology Titanium Powder & Superalloys
entries.thesisShort: Carpenter Technology is the niche specialty alloy leader for jet engine hot-section parts; fiscal Q4 2026 set a record $207 million of quarterly operating income at a 37.8% Specialty Alloys margin, with fiscal 2027 guided to $850-880 million.
entries.thesisLong:
Carpenter Technology occupies the narrowest and most defensible position in specialty metals: the alloys that go into jet engine hot sections, where the material has to survive temperatures near its own melting point and the qualification barrier is close to absolute.

Fiscal Q4 2026 was a record. Quarterly operating income reached $207 million and the core Specialty Alloys Operations segment delivered a 37.8% adjusted operating margin — an industry-leading figure that reflects pricing power rather than volume leverage. Adjusted EPS of $3.23 beat the $3.07 consensus.

Aerospace and defense sales rose 3% sequentially and 17% year over year, reflecting accelerating activity across the aerospace supply chain as Boeing and Airbus push toward higher build rates against a backlog of roughly 16,000 aircraft, while engine manufacturers work to secure supply for both rising production and elevated MRO demand. That dual pull — new build and aftermarket at the same time — is what keeps hot-section alloy demand structurally tight.

The forward guide is where management put its conviction. Fiscal 2027 operating income is guided to $850-880 million, representing 21-25% growth from the record fiscal 2026 result, with $400-430 million of adjusted free cash flow, and the fiscal 2029 target is $1.2-1.3 billion of operating income driven by underlying demand and a brownfield expansion project.

Risks are the standard specialty metals set: commercial aerospace cyclicality, energy-intensive vacuum melt operations, and operational execution on the margin ramp implied by a multi-year target that assumes both volume and mix continue improving.

Elevated engine MRO demand alongside new build
